opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing people miss is that our sense of speed is a poor guide to actual speed. When you're working with an AI system, it *feels* fast. You type a request, and a wall of plausible text or code appears in seconds. That moment of generation is vivid and memorable, so it dominates your impression of the whole task.

But the generation step was rarely the bottleneck. The time goes into the parts that don't feel like "work" in the same way: writing a careful prompt, reading what came back, checking whether it's actually right, noticing the subtle error on line forty, re-prompting, integrating the result into everything else you're doing, and sometimes abandoning the approach and doing it yourself anyway. Those costs are diffuse and easy to forget, while the speedups are concentrated and salient.

There was a nice piece of evidence on this from METR, a randomised trial with experienced open-source developers working in their own codebases. Before the study, they expected AI tools to make them substantially faster. Afterwards, they still believed they'd been sped up. But the measured result was that they'd actually been slower on the tasks where they used AI. I wouldn't over-generalise from one study, since the tools are improving quickly and the result will depend a lot on the kind of work. But the gap between perceived and measured productivity is the striking part, and I'd expect that gap to persist even as the true numbers change.

A second thing people miss is something like Amdahl's law for knowledge work. If AI makes one component of a task ten times faster, but that component was only a third of the total, you don't get a tenfold speedup. You get something much more modest, and the remaining parts, like judgement, coordination, waiting on other people, and deciding what to do in the first place, become the binding constraint. People tend to quote the speedup on the piece that got automated rather than on the whole workflow.

Third, there's a quality dimension that gets folded in silently. Sometimes you finish faster, but what you produce is a bit worse, or you understand it less well. That might be a fine trade, but it's a different claim from "I'm twice as productive," and it can come back to bite you later when you have to maintain or defend the work.

So my advice is simply to measure it. If it matters to you, time some comparable tasks with and without the tools, and look at the whole thing from start to finish, not just the exciting moment where the text appears. I think many people would be surprised in one direction or the other, and either way they'd learn where these tools actually help them, which is the useful thing to know.

r001.rationale: The response says AI-assisted work can leave you understanding the output less well, but it does not state that delegating the task to AI forfeits learning you would gain by doing it yourself.

r002.rationale: The response mentions judgment and deciding what to do as parts of a workflow, but does not say that reflective thinking outside working hours fails to speed up in proportion to AI-assisted work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest thing people miss is that they're measuring the wrong unit. When you ask someone how much AI sped them up, they tend to answer about the task they just did — the piece of code, the draft, the literature summary — and they'll say "that took me an hour instead of three." And that's probably true for that task. But the thing that actually matters is the whole pipeline: how long it took to figure out what to ask for, how long you spent checking the output, how long you spent fixing the bits that were subtly wrong, and whether you then had to redo any downstream work because you trusted something you shouldn't have.

There's a kind of selection effect in how we notice this. The tasks where AI helps a lot are vivid and satisfying, so they stick in memory. The tasks where you spent forty minutes going back and forth with a model and then gave up and did it yourself don't feel like "AI work," so they get mentally filed somewhere else. So your introspective estimate ends up being an average over the successes rather than over everything you tried.

The second thing people miss is that speed-ups on individual tasks don't compose the way you'd expect. If a project has ten steps and AI makes three of them five times faster, you don't get anything like a 5x project. You get something bounded by the other seven. This is just Amdahl's law, and it shows up everywhere — the bottleneck moves to meetings, to waiting on other people, to the thinking you have to do yourself. And often the parts that AI accelerates were never the parts that were actually constraining you.

And then there's something more subtle, which I think is the most interesting one. When a task gets cheaper, you do more of it. You write more code, you explore more alternatives, you produce more drafts. Some of that is genuine extra value, but some of it is just filling the time that was freed up. So the question "how much faster am I?" can have a very different answer from "how much more am I accomplishing?" — and the second question is the one we should actually care about. I've noticed in my own work that AI has changed what I attempt at least as much as how fast I finish things, and that's much harder to put a number on.

I'd also say people underweight the learning effects in both directions. Early on you're slower than you'll eventually be because you haven't learned what the tools are good for. But there's also a possibility that over time you lose some of the skill or the background understanding that would let you catch the model's mistakes — and that's a cost that doesn't show up in any single-task timing at all. It only shows up months later.

So if I had to summarise: measure the project, not the task; count the failures, not just the successes; and ask what you're producing, not just how fast you're going.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a possible loss of skill or background understanding over time, but does not state that delegating tasks to AI forgoes the learning gained by doing them oneself.

r002.rationale: The response discusses project bottlenecks and thinking that AI cannot accelerate, but does not mention reflective thinking outside working hours or say that it fails to speed up proportionally.

astra-6.text:
I think people often focus on the part of the task where the AI is most impressive, rather than on the whole task. You might get a draft in a minute that would have taken you an hour. But you still have to work out what you want to say, check whether the draft is right, and revise it. So a sixtyfold speedup in producing the draft needn’t translate into anything like a sixtyfold speedup in your work.

There’s also a selection effect. We tend to use AI on the tasks where it helps, and then estimate its impact by thinking about those tasks. But to understand how much it speeds up your work overall, you have to include all the things you do where it doesn’t help very much.

And that can change where the bottleneck is. If producing text becomes very cheap, then deciding which text is worth producing, and judging whether it’s any good, may become the things that take most of your time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses checking and revising AI drafts, but does not say delegating work to AI can forgo learning from doing it oneself.

r002.rationale: It discusses bottlenecks in work, but does not mention reflective thinking outside working hours or its pace relative to AI-assisted work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people often focus on how much faster AI makes a particular task, rather than how much faster it makes the whole project. If it makes writing some code ten times faster, that doesn’t mean you finish your work ten times faster. You still have to work out what to build, check whether it works, and fit it together with everything else. The bottleneck moves.

There’s also a distinction between getting an answer and getting an answer you can trust. If you’re working on something where you can immediately recognise a good answer, AI can be tremendously useful. If checking the answer is itself most of the intellectual work, the gain may be much smaller.

But there’s an effect in the other direction, too. You might try things you wouldn’t otherwise have tried because they used to be too costly. So just timing the tasks you already do can miss some of the benefit. What we really want to know is how much more valuable work you can accomplish, at the same standard, over a sustained period.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task speed and checking AI’s answers, but does not say that delegating work to AI can forgo learning gained by doing it yourself.

r002.rationale: The response mentions sustained work and project bottlenecks, but does not discuss reflective thinking outside working hours or say it fails to speed up in proportion to AI-assisted work.
